title: Sedemac's journey: From IIT Bombay lab to a ₹1,000-crore market listing
excerpt: The IIT Bombay deep-tech startup that cracked sensorless commutation crossed ₹1,058 crore in FY26 revenue, then listed at a 13.5% premium — a rare profitable hardware IPO from an academic lab.
body:
• SEDEMAC, founded from an IIT Bombay lab in 2007, crossed ₹1,058 crore in annual revenue in FY26 and listed in March 2026 with a ₹1,087-crore offer for sale at a ~₹5,970-crore valuation.
  • Its integrated starter generators sit inside an estimated 12 to 13 million two-wheelers on Indian roads; five of the country's top 10 selling models use the technology in at least one variant.
  • The company claims to be the first globally to crack sensorless commutation at zero and low speeds — a physics problem the industry had left unsolved for decades.
  • Profitability is its differentiator: roughly ₹200 crore EBITDA and ~40% return on capital employed in FY26, achieved without fresh equity since 2018.

An electronics lab at IIT Bombay rarely produces a listed company. SEDEMAC did exactly that in March 2026, when the deep-tech manufacturer debuted on the stock exchanges with a ₹1,087.45-crore initial public offering — entirely an offer for sale, with no fresh capital raised by the company. Shares listed on March 11 at a 13.5% premium to the upper end of the ₹1,287–1,352 price band, valuing the company at roughly ₹5,970 crore. Anchor investors including HDFC Mutual Fund, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, Goldman Sachs and Invesco came in ahead of the listing.

The market debut capped a near two-decade run that began in 2007–08, when Professor Shashikanth Suryanarayanan — a UC Berkeley PhD who had just joined the IIT Bombay faculty — incorporated the company with his students Amit Dixit and Manish Sharma, and co-founder Pushkaraj Panse. The roots go further back: in 2004, Dixit, a master's student, teamed up with Suryanarayanan on industry-sponsored projects, including a steer-by-wire vehicle for Sona Koyo Steering Systems and an electronic fuel-injection ECU for TVS Motor Company, on combined project budgets of just ₹30–50 lakh.

The physics problem nobody had solved

SEDEMAC's defining breakthrough is sensorless commutation in motor controllers. A motor controller manages power flow between a battery and an electric machine, and to do so it must know the rotor's position — conventionally supplied by a physical sensor. Sensorless commutation estimates that position without one. At high speeds this was understood for decades, but at zero and low speeds the physics turns hostile: the back-EMF phenomenon used for estimation weakens with speed and vanishes at a standstill.

"We are the first company globally, globally, it is a very big statement, that has made as much progress in sensorless commutation as we have," Suryanarayanan says.

The breakthrough did not arrive as a grand plan. Around 2014–15, while developing an integrated starter generator (ISG) for the two-wheeler industry, the team realised the system could be meaningfully improved by solving this problem. In 2018, a TVS moped became the first vehicle to use the system — what Suryanarayanan describes as the world's first sensorless ISG application.

Scale inside a four-player market

What followed was a slow, hard-won adoption curve. SEDEMAC estimates 12 to 13 million vehicles carrying its ISG are now on Indian roads, and five of the country's top 10 selling two-wheelers use the system in at least one variant, including models from TVS, Bajaj and Hero. Another SEDEMAC technology has gone into roughly 50 million vehicles. The company now ships around one million motor controllers every quarter.

Breaking in required displacing entrenched global suppliers in a market where four manufacturers — Honda, Hero, TVS and Bajaj — account for about 85% of sales. SEDEMAC now supplies three of those four. Independent research cited in IPO coverage puts its share at 35% of the domestic ISG ECU market for two- and three-wheelers, and 75–77% of the domestic genset controller segment.

Revenue tells the trajectory: ₹8 crore in 2014, ₹18 crore in 2015, ₹36 crore in 2016 — and ₹1,058 crore by FY26, nearly 30 times the 2016 figure. ISG has been the biggest growth contributor since FY19. The team has grown to roughly 250 engineers, with 60–70% drawn from IITs, NITs and BITS.

Profitability as proof of technology

Suryanarayanan is more emphatic about the bottom line than the top. SEDEMAC reported around ₹200 crore in EBITDA, ₹150 crore in profit before tax and ₹100 crore in profit after tax for FY26, at roughly 40% return on capital employed. His argument: genuine technological differentiation should eventually show up as pricing power and margins.

"If you claim that you are a technology company that has succeeded, how can you not make money?"

— Shashikanth Suryanarayanan, SEDEMAC founder

He qualifies the argument for companies that have reached scale rather than those still investing to establish themselves. But once adoption happens, he argues, advantage should be visible in the economics: "If you do not have strong enough EBITDAs and good ROCE, you are not a technology company. Straight." The capital path backs the claim — Nexus invested ₹2 crore in 2008, and from December 2018 to July 2024 the company raised no fresh equity, funding growth from ₹200 crore to ₹650 crore largely through debt.

What deep tech actually needs

For Suryanarayanan, SEDEMAC's journey depended on two ingredients above all else: extraordinary technical ability, and large, sophisticated customers capable of adopting what those engineers built. "Creators of technology are market creators," he says. "You don't start with, 'Oh, this market is going to grow big.' Therefore, it will grow big or not because of you."

Capital, he places below those two. Investors can enable a business but never create one, he argues: "You can never produce the talent just by throwing some money." His hiring philosophy is unsentimental — top engineers care about the quality of the work and fair reward, not the vision statement — and at SEDEMAC, he says, the strength of an argument outranks hierarchy: "If you're talking nonsense, people will say you're talking nonsense."

He frames India's deep-tech gap as an imagination problem: ecosystems produce excellence when young engineers can see the top of the world inside them. The company now offers one working model of that future, and it is pushing into EV motor controllers, generator controls, commercial-vehicle electronics, power tools and international markets — a broader bet that will test whether the engine that built sensorless commutation can build the next technology too.

nri_angle: SEDEMAC's rise from an IIT Bombay lab is a milestone for the vast Indian-origin engineering diaspora that studied in the same classrooms — and a counterpoint to the services narrative, showing India's technical institutions can spawn original, globally adopted hardware technology.
